GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: This is an old picture by Archimedes: two lengths on a circle that look different always turn out to be the same.
How to play: Drag the point P around the circle with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press Check the lengths to see what stays equal.
Look for the math

Archimedes' Book of Lemmas, Proposition 3, says that if P is anywhere on the circle with base AB, then a point Q chosen so that arc PA equals arc PQ gives a length BQ equal to BD. Drag P and the two green lengths change together; the claim never fails.

Setting up the picture

AB is a diameter of the circle, with centre O. P sits on the circle. N is the point where the line from P dropped straight down meets AB, and D is placed so that N is the middle of AD. The page from 2016 now shows a GeoGebra picture; the old Java applet this page ports used exactly these same points, while its drawn arc was placed with a bounding box centred at A rather than at O. We draw the circle from its centre, as the proposition requires; the construction of N, D, Q and the claim are unchanged.

Why PA and PQ are equal

Equal arcs cut off equal chords, so PA = PQ. That means Q is the other place on the circle that is the same distance from P as A is. Both O and P are equally far from A and Q, so the line OP is the perpendicular bisector of AQ: in other words, Q is the mirror image of A across OP. The logic test uses this reflection and compares it, at every half-degree position of P, with the applet's own method of intersecting the two circles.

Why PA and PD are equal too

Because PN is perpendicular to AB and AN = ND, the line PN is the perpendicular bisector of AD. Any point on that line is equally far from A and D, so PA = PD. Together with PA = PQ this gives PQ = PD, which makes the triangle PQD isosceles: the angles PQD and PDQ are equal.

The last step

A, P, Q and B lie on one circle, so opposite angles of the cyclic quadrilateral add to two right angles. Chasing those angles around, using the equal angles at PQD and PDQ, leaves the angles BQD and BDQ equal. A triangle with two equal angles has two equal sides, so BQ = BD. The logic test checks this at 720 positions of P, plus 400 circles that have been moved, resized and turned: every one passes, including P at A and P at B.

Turn on Show proof lines and Show equal marks, then drag P close to A and close to B: watch which pairs of tick marks stay matched.
